entities.name: National Museum of Anthropology
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The National Museum of Anthropology (Museo Nacional de Antropología, est. 1964, Mexico City — designed by Pedro Ramírez Vázquez) is the most important museum in the Americas for pre-Columbian cultures — the world's largest anthropological museum, with 23 exhibition halls and 600,000+ objects covering 40 millennia of Mexican and Mesoamerican history. The museum's centrepiece is the Aztec Sun Stone (the 'Aztec Calendar'), but its collections span all major Mesoamerican civilisations: Olmec, Maya, Teotihuacan, Toltec, Mixtec, and Aztec.

The museum was opened on 17 September 1964 by President Adolfo López Mateos in Chapultepec Park — one of the world's great park settings for a museum — in a building considered a masterpiece of modernist Mexican architecture. Pedro Ramírez Vázquez's design incorporates pre-Columbian architectural references in a modernist idiom — the central courtyard with its single giant mushroom-shaped column (the tlaloc pillar, 11 metres in diameter, supporting the roof of the entire courtyard) represents a uniquely Mexican fusion of indigenous cultural reference and modernist structural engineering.

The museum's famous January 1985 theft — when five men broke in and removed 140 objects, including a jade Zapotec funeral mask and a Monte Albán funerary urn — and their recovery three years later (most objects intact) is considered one of the greatest art heist recoveries in Mexican cultural history.
